title: Choosing a queue for background jobs
scenario: Comparison and decision-making: three options with costs, must-have and weighted criteria, per-option trade-offs, one load test, and a decision that is explicitly deferred.
audience: Billing team engineers and the architecture review
objective: Compare the three queue options fairly, keep each option's conditions with it, see what the evidence does and does not show, and understand that no option has been chosen yet.

sourceFiles.title: Choosing a queue for background jobs

sections.heading: Choosing a queue for background jobs

units.quote: This note was written for the billing team's architecture review and replaces the earlier draft shared in chat.

omittable.note: About the note itself, not the decision.

units.quote: The billing service runs about 40,000 background jobs a day: rendering invoice PDFs, sending receipt emails and retrying failed webhooks.
Today they run in an in-process worker pool, so a deploy or a crash loses any job that was queued but not yet started.
Last quarter that lost 37 invoice emails that customers had to request again.
Peak load is 600 jobs per minute, during the month-end billing run.
**Option A: managed cloud queue.** A queue service run by our cloud provider.
We send messages to it and workers poll for them; the provider handles storage, scaling and redelivery.
**Option B: self-hosted broker.** A message broker cluster of three virtual machines that we install, patch and monitor ourselves.
**Option C: database job table.** A `jobs` table in the existing billing Postgres database.
Workers claim rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and mark them done.
| Managed cloud queue | $310 | about 2 hours | Priced per million requests; grows with volume |

critical.note: The managed queue's monthly cost and effort.

units.quote: | Self-hosted broker | $540 | about 12 hours | Three VMs plus upgrades and on-call |

critical.note: The broker's monthly cost and effort.

units.quote: | Database job table | $0 extra | about 4 hours | Uses spare capacity on the existing primary |

critical.note: The job table's monthly cost and effort.

units.quote: The managed queue's figure assumes current volume.

critical.note: The $310 holds only at today's volume.

units.quote: At three times today's volume it would be roughly $900 a month, while the broker's cost would stay flat until the cluster needs a fourth machine.
Two criteria are must-haves; an option that fails either is out regardless of its score:

critical.note: Must-haves gate options before any scoring.

units.quote: No job is lost when a worker crashes or the service is deployed.
The queue absorbs 1,800 jobs per minute (three times today's peak) without manual intervention.
The remaining criteria are weighted for scoring:
Operational effort: 40%
Monthly cost: 30%
Developer experience, including local testing: 20%
Portability away from our cloud provider: 10%
Option A needs almost no operational work, and failed messages move to a dead-letter queue automatically.
The catch is that the service delivers each message at least once, so every job handler must be made idempotent before we switch; today only the email handler is.

critical.note: Option A is only safe once every handler is idempotent.

units.quote: It also ties us to one provider's API, and local development needs an emulator that does not support dead-lettering.
Option B gives us priority queues and delayed delivery, which would let month-end invoices jump ahead of webhook retries.
No one on the team has run this broker in production, so the 12 hours a month is an estimate, not a measurement.

critical.note: The broker's effort figure is a guess, not a measurement.

units.quote: Upgrades need a maintenance window.
Option C writes a job in the same transaction as the billing change that causes it, so a job can never be lost between the commit and the enqueue.
That guarantee only covers jobs created inside the billing database transaction; jobs enqueued by the reporting service, which has its own database, would not get it.

critical.note: The transactional guarantee has an exception: the reporting service.

units.quote: Polling also adds read load to the primary database, which is the main risk at month-end.
We load-tested Option C on a staging copy of the database with synthetic jobs.
It sustained 1,200 jobs per minute with a p95 claim latency of 18 ms.
At 2,000 jobs per minute, primary CPU reached 85% and p95 latency rose to 240 ms.
We did not test 1,800 jobs per minute, and the staging copy is about a quarter of production size, so these results may not carry over.

critical.note: The evidence does not cover the required load and may not transfer to production.

units.quote: We have not load-tested Options A or B.

critical.note: Only one option has any evidence.

units.quote: The provider documents throughput far above our peak for Option A, but that is the provider's figure, not ours.
This note does not recommend an option.
The decision is deferred until Option C has been measured at 1,800 jobs per minute on a production-sized database.
Until then, each option carries an open requirement:
Option A: every job handler made idempotent.
Option B: a named owner for broker on-call and upgrades.
Option C: a passing load test at 1,800 jobs per minute.
Priya will bring the load-test result to the next architecture review.

critical.note: The one next step, with its owner.

units.quote: Thanks to everyone who commented on the first draft.
